events.title: Monteverdi's Orfeo Premieres
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Italian composer staged a setting of the Orpheus myth at a ducal palace in a northern Italian city, combining recitative, arias, choruses, and instrumental ritornellos in a way earlier experimental works had only gestured at. The resulting five-act piece is considered the first opera that remains in the regular performance repertoire. Only two printed scores of the work survive.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1607 — Claudio Monteverdi at the court of the Gonzagas in Mantua. The orchestra called for some 40 instruments. The character of Orpheus was sung by tenor Francesco Rasi; the audience was tiny — members of the Accademia degli Invaghiti.

events.title: Bach Dedicates Brandenburg Concertos
events.blurb: A 36-year-old German court composer, looking for a new job, sent a margrave a set of six concerto grossi he had been accumulating over several years. The dedication was effusive; he apologized for the "vast distance between his person and the margrave." The margrave never acknowledged the gift, let alone hired him, and probably never had them performed. The manuscripts sat in a Prussian archive for 128 years before rediscovery.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1721 — Johann Sebastian Bach, addressing Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg. The scores were narrowly rescued from Allied bombing in 1945. The music now exists thanks to a librarian who grabbed them as he fled Leipzig for the Harz mountains.

events.title: Dylan Goes Electric
events.blurb: A 24-year-old folk singer, backed by a ragged rhythm section from the previous night's acquaintance, walked onto the stage of a folk festival on a Rhode Island pier with a sunburst Stratocaster slung low over his shoulder. He played three short electric songs before some boos drowned out the applause. He walked off, returned with his acoustic, and played two more. The event marked, depending on who tells it, the birth of folk-rock or the betrayal of American folk.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1965 — Bob Dylan at the Newport Folk Festival. Pete Seeger, legend says, tried to cut the sound cables with an axe. Seeger later denied it. The songs included "Maggie's Farm" and "Like a Rolling Stone." Dylan's next tour was booed nightly for a year.

events.title: Dark Side of the Moon Released
events.blurb: An English progressive rock band released a conceptual album about madness, mortality, capitalism, and the passage of time, tracks flowing into each other via tape loops of spoken voices, heartbeats, and cash registers. The cover was a simple black triangular prism refracting white light into a rainbow. The album would stay on the Billboard 200 for 741 consecutive weeks — more than 14 years — a record that has never been approached.
events.revealBlurb: March 1, 1973 — Pink Floyd. Recorded at Abbey Road using then-new 16-track technology and Roger Waters' theatrical sensibility. The album has sold over 45 million copies. The "we don't need no education" band followed eight years later with another cultural juggernaut, The Wall.

events.title: Thriller Released
events.blurb: A 24-year-old singer released his sixth studio album, a collection of nine tracks deliberately designed so every one could be a single. The 14-minute title track's horror-film music video, featuring choreographed zombie dancing, premiered the following December on a cable channel that had until recently been reluctant to play Black artists. The album became, and remains, the best-selling album of all time.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 1982 — Michael Jackson, produced by Quincy Jones. It has sold over 70 million copies worldwide. The moonwalk, which Jackson debuted performing "Billie Jean" at Motown's 25th-anniversary TV special 3.5 months after release, was not actually his invention.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish instrument maker, repairing a model of a 50-year-old atmospheric engine for a university natural philosophy class, realized its efficiency was fatally compromised by repeatedly heating and cooling the same cylinder. His solution — a separate condensing vessel — cut fuel consumption by 75 percent. Patented four years later, the improved engine could be sited anywhere, not only beside a coal pit, and became the prime mover of 19th-century industry.
events.revealBlurb: 1765 insight; January 5, 1769 patent — James Watt. His decade-long partnership with Birmingham industrialist Matthew Boulton commercialized the engine. The unit of power is named for him. "Horsepower" was also his invention, a marketing metric.

events.title: US Transcontinental Railroad Completed
events.blurb: Officials drove a ceremonial golden spike into a rail tie at a desolate spot in Utah, joining rails built eastward from Sacramento by Chinese labourers and rails built westward from the Missouri River by Irish labourers. Travel from New York to San Francisco, previously a six-month journey by wagon or ship, now took a week. The two companies, a state-subsidized joint venture, had raced each other for six years; the route had been set by the Lincoln administration in 1862.
events.revealBlurb: May 10, 1869 — Promontory Summit, Utah. The joining rails were two: Central Pacific from the west, Union Pacific from the east. The spike ceremony was telegraphed to the rest of the country; the "Done" message was the first cross-country news bulletin. The Chinese workers who had done most of the hardest labour were not invited to the ceremony.

events.title: Bell Patents Telephone
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Scottish-born American inventor was granted a patent on "the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically." Three days later he made the first recognized telephone call in his Boston laboratory, summoning his assistant from the next room. The patent, filed the same morning as a rival inventor's competing application, would become the most valuable patent ever issued by the US government.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1876 — Alexander Graham Bell. The first call: "Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you." The rival, Elisha Gray, filed his caveat a few hours later; legal battles continued for years. American Telephone & Telegraph, founded on Bell's patent, became the largest corporation in the world.

events.title: Edison Invents Phonograph
events.blurb: A 30-year-old American inventor shouted the first verse of "Mary Had a Little Lamb" into the horn of a machine he had built at his New Jersey laboratory, then cranked a handle to make the machine play his words back to him. Recording sound — not just transmitting it instantaneously as the telephone did — had never been done before. The device, a tinfoil-cylinder phonograph, would be followed by commercial wax-cylinder versions by the end of the decade.
events.revealBlurb: November 21, 1877 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. The original tinfoil phonograph could replay a recording only a few times before the foil wore out. The machine astonished audiences when Edison demonstrated it at the Scientific American office a week later.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: British Parliament Passes the Stamp Act
events.blurb: Parliament enacted a sweeping tax requiring colonists to purchase revenue stamps for newspapers, legal documents, almanacs, and even playing cards — the first direct tax Britain had ever levied on its American colonies. Outcry was immediate and visceral: colonial assemblies passed resolutions of protest, merchants organized boycotts, and a new network of radicals calling themselves the Sons of Liberty took to the streets.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1765 — London. The tax was repealed the following year under merchant pressure, but Parliament simultaneously passed the Declaratory Act asserting its absolute right to tax the colonies "in all cases whatsoever." The colonists celebrated the repeal and mostly ignored the Declaratory Act — for about a decade.

events.title: Boston Massacre
events.blurb: A confrontation between a hostile crowd of several hundred colonists and a squad of nine British soldiers on a snow-covered Boston street ended with the soldiers firing into the mob, killing five men. The deaths — including Crispus Attucks, a formerly enslaved sailor of African and Indigenous descent — were immediately weaponized as propaganda, with Paul Revere producing an engraving that circulated throughout the colonies.
events.revealBlurb: March 5, 1770 — King Street, Boston. John Adams, who would become America's second president, defended the British soldiers in court and won acquittals for six of the eight — calling it one of the best things he ever did for his country. Attucks is often called the first American to die for independence.

events.title: Cornwallis Surrenders at Yorktown
events.blurb: A British army of 8,000 men under a peer of the realm, trapped on a Virginia peninsula by a combined Franco-American land force and blocked from the Chesapeake by a French fleet, surrendered after a three-week siege. The British commander, reportedly feigning illness, sent a deputy to the surrender ceremony; his band played a tune called "The World Turned Upside Down." The war dragged on in minor engagements for two more years but the outcome was no longer in doubt.
events.revealBlurb: October 19, 1781 — Lord Cornwallis surrenders to General George Washington and Comte de Rochambeau at Yorktown, Virginia. The French navy's blockade, commanded by Admiral de Grasse, decided the siege. Formal peace negotiations began within months.

events.title: Storming of the Bastille
events.blurb: A mob of several thousand Parisians, enraged by the dismissal of a popular finance minister and rumours of royal military preparations, stormed a royal fortress prison on the city's eastern edge in search of gunpowder stored there. The garrison surrendered after a bloody four-hour assault; the commandant was murdered and his head carried on a pike through the streets. The prison itself held only seven prisoners. The date became the French national holiday.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1789 — the Bastille. Seven prisoners: four forgers, two lunatics, one aristocrat imprisoned by his family. Marquis de Launay, the commandant, is the famous head on the pike. Parisians began demolishing the fortress the next morning; it was fully down within three months.

events.title: Congress of Vienna
events.blurb: Diplomats from Europe's surviving great powers, meeting for nine months at the Austrian imperial capital while Napoleon was on Elba, produced a settlement redrawing the political map of post-Napoleonic Europe. The Austrian host, a canny foreign minister, aimed to construct a conservative "balance of power" that would suppress revolutionary politics and last a century. The Congress's territorial settlements, with notable adjustments, largely did.
events.revealBlurb: Final Act signed June 9, 1815 — held at Metternich's Vienna. The Congress technically continued its formal sessions even during Napoleon's Hundred Days return. It invented the quartet-conference format that would evolve into the League of Nations and the United Nations.

events.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion Published
events.blurb: A German mathematician published two laws describing how planets orbit the Sun: first, that orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus; second, that a line from the planet to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times — meaning planets move faster when close to the Sun. A third law, relating orbital period to distance, followed ten years later, providing the first precise mathematical description of the solar system.
events.revealBlurb: 1609 (laws 1&2) and 1619 (law 3) — Johannes Kepler derived the laws from the most precise observational data in the world, collected by Tycho Brahe. Brahe had guarded the data obsessively and refused to share it; Kepler obtained it only after Brahe's sudden death. He later calculated that Brahe may have died from a burst bladder after refusing to leave a banquet to use the lavatory.

events.title: Periodic Table of Elements Published
events.blurb: A Russian chemist arranged the sixty-three known elements into a table ordered by atomic weight, discovering that chemical properties recurred in a regular pattern. He boldly left gaps for elements he predicted did not yet exist, specifying their likely weights and properties in advance — predictions that proved startlingly accurate when the missing elements were found over the following two decades.
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1869 — Dmitri Mendeleev reportedly saw the complete arrangement in a dream and woke to write it down, though historians treat this story sceptically. He sent a one-page summary to chemists across Europe before the formal presentation. Germanium, gallium, and scandium were discovered later, matching his predictions closely.

events.title: Radioactivity Discovered
events.blurb: A French physicist studying uranium salts placed a wrapped photographic plate in a drawer alongside a uranium sample during several cloudy days, expecting to run a sunlight experiment later. When he developed the plate anyway, he found a sharp image — proving the uranium was spontaneously emitting invisible radiation with no external energy source, a phenomenon no existing theory could explain.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1896 — Henri Becquerel announced to the Academy of Sciences that the image was "very distinct." The discovery was accidental: bad weather cancelled his planned sunlight experiment. He initially thought it was a variant of X-rays; it took the Curies to show radioactivity was a property of the atom itself.

events.title: Endosymbiotic Theory Published
events.blurb: A paper proposed that the energy-producing mitochondria and photosynthetic chloroplasts inside complex cells were originally free-living bacteria that had been engulfed by a host cell and retained over billions of years — a radical claim that the cell's most vital structures were once independent organisms. The paper had been rejected by approximately fifteen journals before finding a publisher.
events.revealBlurb: June 1967 — Lynn Margulis submitted the paper under her married surname Sagan; it became one of biology's most-cited papers after decades of derision. Her critics called it "too fantastic." When the hypothesis was tested by comparing DNA in mitochondria to bacterial DNA in the 1980s, it matched almost exactly.

events.title: Higgs Boson Announced
events.blurb: At a packed seminar, two independent experimental teams working at the world's largest particle accelerator announced the observation of a new particle consistent with the long-predicted Higgs boson — the quantum field excitation that gives other fundamental particles their mass. The discovery completed the standard model of particle physics, confirming a prediction made nearly fifty years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 2012 — Peter Higgs, who had predicted the boson in 1964, was in the audience and reportedly wept. The two experiments — ATLAS and CMS — had been run in blind competition to avoid bias. Higgs and François Englert shared the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year.

events.title: Iron Curtain Speech
events.blurb: A former British prime minister, speaking at a small college in Missouri at the invitation of the sitting U.S. president, declared that an impenetrable barrier had descended across the European continent from the Baltic to the Adriatic. The phrase he coined to describe it entered geopolitical vocabulary within hours.
events.revealBlurb: March 5, 1946 — Winston Churchill at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri. Truman sat on stage behind him. The 5,000-word speech was titled "The Sinews of Peace," but nobody remembers that part.

events.title: Stalin Dies
events.blurb: Found unconscious on the floor of his dacha outside Moscow after a late-night dinner with colleagues, a dictator who had ruled for nearly three decades lingered for four days before dying of a brain hemorrhage. His inner circle, terrified of waking him, had delayed calling doctors for many hours. His state funeral drew crowds so large that dozens were trampled.
events.revealBlurb: March 5, 1953 — Joseph Stalin, 74, at his Kuntsevo dacha. He'd spent the previous evening screening American westerns. His death unleashed a succession struggle; Khrushchev prevailed and began the cautious thaw.

events.title: SDI Announced
events.blurb: In a televised address from the Oval Office, a U.S. president proposed a space-based missile defense shield intended to render nuclear weapons "impotent and obsolete." Critics dubbed it "Star Wars" and scientists called it technically unachievable. Whatever its technical merits, the announcement terrified the Kremlin and forced Soviet planners to contemplate a ruinous new arms race they could not afford.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 1983 — Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative. It never produced a working system, but it contributed to Soviet economic exhaustion. Some historians credit SDI with accelerating Gorbachev's arms-control pivot by years.

events.title: Chernobyl Disaster
events.blurb: During a safety test at the No. 4 reactor of a Ukrainian nuclear power plant, a power surge, flawed reactor design, and operator errors combined to blow the 1,000-tonne reactor lid off the building and send a radioactive plume across Europe. Swedish sensors detected the contamination before Moscow admitted anything had happened. The exclusion zone around the plant remains largely uninhabited nearly forty years on.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 1986 — 1:23 AM. Two workers died in the initial explosion; 28 firefighters and operators died of acute radiation poisoning in the months after. Roughly 350,000 people were permanently evacuated. Cleanup cost the USSR an estimated 18 billion rubles.

events.title: INF Treaty Signed
events.blurb: At a White House ceremony, the American and Soviet leaders signed a treaty requiring both sides to destroy every intermediate-range nuclear missile they possessed — the first arms-control agreement that actually cut existing weapons rather than capping their growth. Within three years, 2,692 missiles had been verifiably dismantled.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1987 — Reagan and Gorbachev. Both Pershing IIs and SS-20s were eliminated. The treaty was abandoned in 2019 after mutual accusations of cheating, ending a 32-year cornerstone of European security.

events.title: Euclid's Elements Written
events.blurb: A 13-book mathematical treatise organised geometry, number theory, and proportion into a rigorous deductive system built from five simple axioms and five postulates, from which hundreds of theorems were derived by logical proof alone. The work became the model for mathematical reasoning for more than two thousand years and remained a standard university textbook in parts of Europe into the twentieth century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 300 BCE — almost nothing is known about Euclid himself; even his birthdate is unknown. The Elements is the second most-printed book in history after the Bible. One of its five postulates — the parallel postulate — resisted proof for two thousand years; mathematicians who tried to derive it instead invented non-Euclidean geometry.

events.title: Mendel's Laws of Inheritance Published
events.blurb: After eight years of cross-breeding pea plants and counting roughly 29,000 offspring, an Austrian monk published statistical ratios showing that heritable traits are passed in discrete units — dominant and recessive — and that different traits are inherited independently of one another. The paper described the mathematical foundations of heredity without any knowledge of chromosomes or DNA.
events.revealBlurb: 1866 — the paper was presented at two meetings in 1865 and published a year later, then ignored for 34 years. When three European botanists independently rediscovered the same ratios in 1900 and searched the prior literature, they all found Mendel's paper at the same time. He had died sixteen years earlier.

events.title: Special Relativity Paper Published
events.blurb: A 30-page paper demolished the concept of absolute time, arguing that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion, and that simultaneity, length, and mass all depend on relative velocity. The paper contained no citations, because its author — a patent clerk working in his spare time — had arrived at the theory by pure thought experiment.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1905 — one of four papers the same author submitted to Annalen der Physik that year, including one on Brownian motion and one that would later win the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. The mass-energy equivalence paper (E=mc²) followed two months later.

events.title: Uncertainty Principle Formulated
events.blurb: A paper established that it is fundamentally impossible to know both the exact position and exact momentum of a quantum particle simultaneously — the more precisely one is measured, the less precisely the other can be known, not because of measurement limitations but as a feature of nature itself. The principle implied that determinism at the subatomic scale was not merely unknown but unknowable.
events.revealBlurb: March 1927 — Werner Heisenberg derived the uncertainty principle while working alone in Copenhagen, having sent Niels Bohr on vacation. Bohr returned and disputed the physical interpretation, sparking weeks of argument. Albert Einstein spent years devising thought experiments to disprove the principle; Bohr refuted each one.

events.title: Neutron Discovered
events.blurb: A British physicist bombarded beryllium with alpha particles and detected a neutral radiation that could knock protons out of paraffin wax with remarkable force. Reasoning that gamma rays lacked the energy for such collisions, he concluded the radiation must consist of uncharged particles with roughly the mass of a proton — completing the basic structure of the atomic nucleus.
events.revealBlurb: February 27, 1932 — James Chadwick completed the decisive experiments in under two weeks. He mailed a letter to Nature titled "Possible Existence of a Neutron." Frédéric and Irène Joliot-Curie had the same data a month earlier but misidentified what they had found. Chadwick won the Nobel Prize in 1935.

events.title: Freedom Riders Depart
events.blurb: Thirteen volunteers — seven Black, six white — boarded buses in Washington, D.C. bound for New Orleans to test a recent Supreme Court ruling outlawing segregated interstate travel facilities. In Alabama their bus was firebombed outside Anniston and the riders beaten bloody by a mob in Birmingham. They kept riding. Subsequent waves continued through the summer.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1961 — sponsored by CORE. A 21-year-old John Lewis was among them and had his skull fractured. Attorney General Robert Kennedy called for a "cooling-off period;" CORE leader James Farmer replied: "We've been cooling off for 100 years."

events.title: March on Washington
events.blurb: A quarter-million Americans — three-quarters Black, a quarter white — gathered between the Washington and Lincoln Memorials on the 100th anniversary summer of the Emancipation Proclamation to demand the passage of civil-rights legislation then stalled in Congress. The event's closing address, given on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, contained a phrase repeated in eight paragraphs: "I have a dream."
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1963. MLK's prepared text did not contain "I have a dream" — Mahalia Jackson, behind him on the dais, shouted "Tell them about the dream, Martin!" and he ad-libbed the most famous passage. The Justice Department had 4,000 troops on standby in case of violence. None was needed.

events.title: Bloody Sunday in Selma
events.blurb: Six hundred civil-rights marchers, demanding federal protection for Black voting rights, set out from a small Alabama city to walk 87 kilometres to the state capital. On the Edmund Pettus Bridge at the edge of town, state troopers and a sheriff's posse on horseback charged them with clubs and tear gas. Televised images of a beaten John Lewis shocked the nation into action.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1965 — Selma, Alabama. Lewis's skull was fractured. Lyndon Johnson appeared before a joint session of Congress eight days later to introduce the Voting Rights Act, closing with the movement's own anthem: "We shall overcome."

events.title: Fair Housing Act Signed
events.blurb: One week after the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., Congress passed and the president signed legislation outlawing discrimination in the sale, rental, and financing of housing. The bill had been stalled for two years; King's death and the rioting that followed pushed it through. It closed the third major gap in civil rights law, after employment (1964) and voting (1965).
events.revealBlurb: April 11, 1968 — Lyndon Johnson. Informally called the Civil Rights Act of 1968. Enforcement remained toothless for decades; the Department of Housing and Urban Development did not gain meaningful investigation powers until the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988.

events.title: MLK Day Signed
events.blurb: After 15 years of advocacy by civil rights leaders, Congress passed and the president signed legislation establishing the third Monday of January as a federal holiday honoring the slain civil rights leader. The fight to pass it had drawn bitter opposition from some senators, including one who conducted a 16-day filibuster. It became the first federal holiday commemorating an African-American.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 1983 — Ronald Reagan. Arizona voters rejected recognizing the holiday in 1990; the NFL moved the 1993 Super Bowl from Phoenix in response, and the state reversed course. New Hampshire, the last holdout, adopted it in 1999.

events.title: World Wide Web Proposed
events.blurb: A British software engineer working at a Swiss particle-physics laboratory circulated an internal memo proposing a distributed hypertext information management system that would link documents across different computers. His supervisor scribbled "Vague, but exciting" across the top and approved further work. The project would take two more years to become a working system.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1989 — Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. His supervisor was Mike Sendall. Berners-Lee never sought patents on his web protocols; he believed the only way they'd spread was to give them away. Queen Elizabeth II knighted him in 2004.

events.title: Yahoo! Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford electrical engineering PhD students who had spent a year maintaining a website called "Jerry and David's guide to the World Wide Web" — a manually curated directory of interesting sites — incorporated their hobby as a business. They'd rename it with a word from Gulliver's Travels meaning an uncouth, rude person. For most of the decade, it was the default homepage of the internet.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1995 — Jerry Yang and David Filo. The name is officially a backronym: "Yet Another Hierarchical Officious Oracle." They turned down a $44.6 billion acquisition offer from Microsoft in 2008; Verizon eventually bought the husk for $4.48 billion in 2017.

events.title: Netscape IPO
events.blurb: A 16-month-old Silicon Valley company that had distributed free web browsers and had never turned a profit went public at $28 a share, opened at $71, and closed its first trading day at $58.25. Its 24-year-old co-founder was suddenly worth $58 million on paper. Wall Street had discovered the internet, and the next five years of stock-market mania had a starting gun.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1995 — Netscape Communications. Co-founder Marc Andreessen ended up on the cover of Time two years later with the caption "The Kid Who Tamed the Web." Microsoft's bundled Internet Explorer would eventually kill Netscape; the company sold to AOL in 1999.

events.title: Google Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford PhD students filed articles of incorporation for a search-engine company they had been developing in a dormitory and a rented garage in suburban California. Their algorithm, unlike those of competitors, ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them. They would never graduate. Their search index contained 60 million pages when they incorporated; it contains hundreds of billions today.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 1998 — Larry Page and Sergey Brin. The name is a misspelling of "googol," the mathematical term for 10^100. Their initial financial backer, Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim, wrote a $100,000 check to "Google Inc." before the company formally existed.

events.title: Twitter's First Tweet
events.blurb: A 29-year-old podcasting-company engineer tested a prototype microblogging platform the team had built in two weeks as a side project, posting the five-word message "just setting up my twttr." Users were limited to 140 characters, the carrier limit for SMS text messages, since the service was originally designed to be usable by phone text. Within four years the service would be blamed — and credited — for upending journalism, politics, and activism.
events.revealBlurb: March 21, 2006 — Jack Dorsey's first tweet. Co-founders included Biz Stone, Noah Glass, and Evan Williams. Elon Musk bought the company for $44 billion in 2022 and renamed it X the following year. Dorsey's original tweet was auctioned as an NFT for $2.9 million in 2021.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: Saladin Retakes Jerusalem
events.blurb: A Kurdish Muslim sultan, having crushed a Crusader field army three months earlier at the Horns of Hattin, accepted the peaceful surrender of the holy city from its desperate defenders after an eight-day siege. In contrast to the bloody Frankish sack of the city 88 years earlier, he permitted ransomed Christians to leave with their possessions and freed many who could not pay. News of the fall triggered the Third Crusade.
events.revealBlurb: October 2, 1187 — Saladin. His reputation for chivalry, magnified by his later adversary Richard the Lionheart, made him a hero of medieval European literature despite being its opponent. Dante placed him in Limbo rather than Hell.

events.title: Avignon Papacy Begins
events.blurb: A French-born pope, under pressure from the French king and unable to safely reside in Rome because of factional warfare among Italian noble families, transferred the papal court across the Alps to a southern French town on the Rhône. For the next 68 years, seven successive popes — all French — would rule the Western church from there, deeply compromising papal prestige.
events.revealBlurb: 1309 — Pope Clement V. Critics called it the "Babylonian Captivity of the Church." The papacy returned to Rome in 1377, only to split almost immediately into rival popes in Rome and Avignon.

events.title: Rome Enters Its First War Against Carthage
events.blurb: A dispute over the Sicilian city of Messana drew Rome and Carthage into twenty-three years of fighting — the longest continuous conflict the Mediterranean world had yet seen. Rome, which began the war without a single warship capable of engaging Carthage's navy, built a fleet of 120 vessels in sixty days by copying a wrecked Carthaginian quinquereme plank by plank.
events.revealBlurb: 264 BCE, Sicily. Rome's main naval innovation was the corvus, a spiked boarding bridge that dropped onto enemy ships and let soldiers fight a naval battle on foot. It worked brilliantly until several storms sank the fleets that carried it.

events.title: The First Triumvirate
events.blurb: Julius Caesar secretly brokered a private political alliance with Rome's two most powerful men: Gnaeus Pompey, celebrated general of the East, and Marcus Crassus, the wealthiest man in Roman history. The three agreed to combine their networks and veto power to dominate legislation; the alliance had no legal standing, no name, and no public announcement.
events.revealBlurb: Late 60 BCE, Rome. Crassus, reportedly worth 200 million sesterces, once claimed no man was truly rich unless he could afford to maintain an army from his own pocket. He would later die at the Battle of Carrhae when, according to legend, the Parthians poured molten gold down his throat.

events.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
events.blurb: A group of Roman senators led by Cassius and Brutus surrounded the dictator in the Theatre of Pompey and stabbed him twenty-three times. A later physician concluded only one wound was fatal; the man fell at the base of a statue of his former rival, Pompey himself.
events.revealBlurb: The Ides of March, 44 BCE. Caesar had been warned by a soothsayer to "beware the Ides of March" and laughed it off the same morning. His last words, "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare — ancient sources quote him saying "You too, child?" in Greek.

events.title: Death of Marcus Aurelius
events.blurb: The philosopher-emperor Marcus Aurelius died of illness at the Danubian frontier, most likely at Vindobona, at the age of 58 after nineteen years of near-constant warfare against Germanic tribes. He chose to pass the empire to his biological son Commodus rather than adopt a capable successor, ending the run of four successive emperors who had done exactly that.
events.revealBlurb: March 17, 180 CE. Marcus kept a private notebook of philosophical reflections — the Meditations — with no apparent intention of publication. One entry reads: "Loss is nothing else but change, and change is Nature's delight." He died of the same plague he had spent a decade governing around.

events.title: Caracalla's Citizenship Edict
events.blurb: Emperor Caracalla issued a decree granting full Roman citizenship to every free person throughout the empire, erasing a 700-year distinction between citizen and non-citizen that had shaped Roman law, military service, and taxation. Modern historians debate whether the primary motive was ideological universalism or a straightforward need to expand the tax base.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 212 CE. Caracalla's full name — Marcus Aurelius Severus Antoninus — was a collection of borrowed dynastic brands. "Caracalla" was the nickname Romans gave him, after a Gallic hooded cloak he popularised. He had his brother and co-emperor Geta killed months before signing this edict.

events.title: Great Chicago Fire
events.blurb: A fire started in a barn on a windy autumn evening in the second-largest U.S. metropolis and burned for 27 hours, destroying 17,500 buildings across 8.5 square kilometres of the central business district and killing around 300 people. A third of the city's population was left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: October 8-10, 1871 — Chicago. The Mrs. O'Leary's cow story is almost certainly a fabrication invented by a reporter who later confessed. On the very same day, the deadlier Peshtigo fire in Wisconsin killed 1,500+ people but is largely forgotten.

events.title: Hindenburg Disaster
events.blurb: A German passenger airship, the largest aircraft ever flown, caught fire as it approached its mooring mast at a New Jersey naval air station, and was consumed in less than 40 seconds. 36 of the 97 people on board died, along with one ground crew member. A radio reporter's anguished live commentary — "Oh, the humanity!" — entered popular idiom.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1937 — Lakehurst, NJ. The reporter was Herbert Morrison; he was actually there to record for later broadcast and didn't expect to be on air. The disaster effectively killed the commercial airship industry overnight.

events.title: Mount St. Helens Eruption
events.blurb: A Pacific Northwest volcano that had been swelling a grotesque 150-metre bulge on its north flank for two months underwent a catastrophic lateral blast triggered by an earthquake. The collapse produced the largest landslide in recorded history, flattening 600 square kilometres of forest and killing 57 people, including a stubborn innkeeper who refused to evacuate.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1980 — Washington State, USA. The innkeeper was Harry R. Truman, 83, who kept pets and a collection of bourbon at his lodge and became a folk hero for his refusal to leave. His body was never found.

events.title: Tōhoku Earthquake & Fukushima
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the Pacific coast of northern Japan triggered tsunami waves up to 40 metres high that killed some 19,700 people and swamped the seawalls of a coastal nuclear plant. Three reactor cores melted down in the following days, contaminating 337 square kilometres of surrounding countryside. 165,000 people were displaced; many never returned.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2011 — 2:46 PM local time. The quake was so powerful it shifted Earth's axis by about 17 centimetres and shortened the day by 1.8 microseconds. The plant's operator, TEPCO, had been warned about tsunami risk years earlier and ignored it.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Declared
events.blurb: The World Health Organization, having watched a novel coronavirus spread from a single city to 114 countries in ten weeks, formally upgraded its assessment from epidemic to pandemic. Within days, much of the world entered some form of lockdown — schools shut, flights grounded, stock markets crashed. Before vaccines arrived a year later, it would kill millions.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2020 — WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. The first known case had been reported in Wuhan in early December 2019. Official global death toll exceeded 7 million; excess mortality studies suggest the real number is closer to 20 million.

events.title: Alam Ara Released — India's First Talkie
events.blurb: Police were deployed outside Majestic Cinema in Bombay that afternoon because the crowds gathering to hear a Hindi film speak for the first time overwhelmed the streets. The fantasy-romance had seven songs, making it arguably the first Bollywood musical; screenings sold out continuously for eight weeks, and the print of the film has since been completely lost.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1931 — directed by Ardeshir Irani. The film was shot in just 40 days. Every surviving account describes the audience's shock at hearing dialogue emerge from the screen, many reportedly weeping.

events.title: Kalidas Released — First Tamil Talkie
events.blurb: A mythological musical about the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa opened at Kinema Central in Madras on Diwali and became simultaneously the first sound film in Tamil and the first in Telugu — the hero singing in Telugu, the heroine speaking Tamil, a third actor delivering dialogue in Hindi, making it a multilingual sound experiment disguised as a devotional drama.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1931 — directed by H.M. Reddy, just months after Alam Ara introduced sound to India. A young actor billed only as L.V. Prasad played a cameo; he would later become one of South India's most powerful film producers. The film is now preserved at the National Film Archive.

events.title: First Filmfare Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: A British-origin film magazine inaugurated India's first popular film awards at Bombay's Metro Theatre with only five categories, winners chosen through postal ballot by readers, and a chief guest who was the US Ambassador to India. The trophy — a black-painted female figure — later became among the most recognisable objects in the entire industry and came to be known, simply, as the Black Lady.
events.revealBlurb: March 21, 1954 — then called the "Clare Awards" after a recently deceased film critic. Best Film went to Bimal Roy's Do Bigha Zamin; Dilip Kumar won Best Actor for Daag. The ceremony's postal-ballot system meant the public, not critics, decided the winners — a populist structure the awards kept for decades.

events.title: Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai Released
events.blurb: A double-role romantic thriller built around a completely unknown actor — son of its director — became the highest-grossing Hindi film of the year and won 92 awards across ceremonies, a figure the Guinness World Records certified as a record for any single film. The overnight stardom it generated was so total that magazine covers, television specials, and public hysteria followed within days.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 2000 — directed by Rakesh Roshan, launching his son Hrithik. The film began production before Hrithik had done a single screen test beyond his father's living room. His dancing in the title track introduced a new male movement vocabulary to Bollywood that choreographers have referenced ever since.

events.title: "Naatu Naatu" Wins Academy Award
events.blurb: A Telugu period action film about two real freedom fighters reimagined as friends on opposite sides of a colonial conflict produced a seven-minute dance sequence that, when performed live at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, brought an Oscars audience to its feet. The song became the first from an Indian film to win the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 2023 — the 95th Academy Awards. Composer M.M. Keeravani and lyricist Chandrabose won. Director S.S. Rajamouli's RRR had not been submitted as India's official Oscar entry — it qualified independently through its US distributor. Singers Rahul Sipligunj and Kaala Bhairava performed barefoot on the Oscars stage.

events.title: Boston Tea Party
events.blurb: That winter night, some 116 colonists disguised as Mohawk warriors boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the water, destroying approximately £10,000 worth of merchandise. The targeted destruction was a direct protest against the Tea Act, which granted the company a monopoly while taxing colonial consumers.
events.revealBlurb: December 16, 1773 — Boston Harbor. Not a single participant was ever prosecuted. Britain's furious response — the Coercive Acts, which colonists renamed the Intolerable Acts — did more to unify colonial resistance than the tea party itself. The name "Boston Tea Party" wasn't coined until decades later.

events.title: Battle of New Orleans
events.blurb: General Andrew Jackson's patchwork army of Tennessee frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, free Black soldiers, Choctaw warriors, and pirates under Jean Lafitte decisively routed an 8,000-strong British force attempting to seize New Orleans, killing or wounding roughly 2,000 redcoats while suffering fewer than 70 American casualties. The lopsided victory made Jackson a national hero and propelled him to the presidency.
events.revealBlurb: January 8, 1815 — Chalmette, Louisiana. The Treaty of Ghent ending the War of 1812 had been signed 15 days earlier — news hadn't arrived. The battle had zero effect on the war's official outcome but enormous effect on American mythology and Jackson's political career.

events.title: Missouri Compromise Signed
events.blurb: President James Monroe signed legislation admitting Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state simultaneously, preserving the Senate balance between slave and free states, and drawing an invisible line across the continent at latitude 36°30' north — prohibiting slavery in all remaining territory of the Louisiana Purchase above that line.
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1820 — Washington, D.C. Thomas Jefferson, then 76, called the Missouri debate "a fire bell in the night" that terrified him. The 36°30' line held for 34 years before the Kansas-Nebraska Act erased it in 1854.

events.title: Caning of Senator Charles Sumner
events.blurb: Representative Preston Brooks of South Carolina strode onto the Senate floor and beat Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts unconscious with a metal-topped gutta-percha cane, inflicting such severe head injuries that Sumner could not return to his seat for over three years. The assault came two days after Sumner delivered a blistering antislavery speech mocking Brooks's cousin; Massachusetts left Sumner's empty desk on display as a rebuke.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1856 — U.S. Senate chamber. Brooks resigned, was immediately re-elected by South Carolina, and received commemorative canes inscribed "Hit Him Again." Sumner's empty desk served as visible propaganda for the antislavery cause for three years. The incident convinced many Northerners that slavery corrupted men beyond reason.

events.title: COVID-19 National Emergency Declared
events.blurb: President Donald Trump declared a national emergency, unlocking $50 billion in federal disaster funds to respond to the coronavirus pandemic, which had by then spread to 49 states and killed dozens of Americans. The pandemic would ultimately claim over 1.1 million American lives — more than any war in the country's history — and shut down schools, businesses, and public life for over a year.
events.revealBlurb: March 13, 2020 — The White House. The first confirmed U.S. case had been detected just 53 days earlier. Within weeks, American unemployment reached 14.7% — the highest since the Great Depression — as roughly 22 million jobs vanished in two months.

events.title: Battleship Potemkin Released
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet director released a 75-minute silent film dramatizing a 1905 mutiny on a Russian imperial battleship. Its centerpiece, a massacre sequence on a flight of stone stairs in the Black Sea port city of Odessa, introduced a style of rapid associative editing that reshaped 20th-century cinema. A baby's pram bounces downward through the gunfire in a shot that has been quoted by dozens of later filmmakers.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 1925 — Sergei Eisenstein. The Odessa Steps massacre is fictional; no such event occurred in 1905. The pram shot has been homaged in The Untouchables, Brazil, and The Simpsons. Joseph Goebbels reportedly called the film "a marvelous film without equal."

events.title: Breathless Released
events.blurb: A 29-year-old French film critic turned director released a 90-minute crime film about a petty thief on the run in Paris with his American girlfriend, shot on handheld camera using natural light, jump cuts, and improvised dialogue. The film's insouciant rulebreaking embodied a new generation of European filmmaking, christened the "Nouvelle Vague" by a critic five years earlier. It made its star into the archetype of post-war cool.
events.revealBlurb: March 16, 1960 — Jean-Luc Godard, starring Jean-Paul Belmondo and Jean Seberg. The famously jarring jump-cuts emerged from an editing crisis: the film was too long and Godard simply removed shots rather than shorten scenes.

events.title: The Godfather Released
events.blurb: A 32-year-old American director of partial Italian descent, working on his third feature, released a 175-minute adaptation of a recent mass-market novel about an Italian-American crime family. His studio had imposed cast, budget, and length conditions throughout production; it had also tried to fire him multiple times. The film grossed more than any previous picture in history, won Best Picture, and launched decades of imitators that have never quite matched it.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1972 — Francis Ford Coppola. Marlon Brando's sagging jowls were created with dental plumpers; Al Pacino's casting was fought bitterly by Paramount executives who wanted Ryan O'Neal. The horse's head was real — acquired from a dog-food plant.

events.title: Apocalypse Now Released
events.blurb: An American director released a 153-minute film loosely adapting Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" to the context of the Vietnam War, shot over 238 days in the Philippines through a typhoon that destroyed much of the set, an on-set heart attack for his leading man, and a drug-fueled spiral for his support cast. He screened a rough cut at Cannes with the warning: "My film is not about Vietnam. My film is Vietnam."
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1979 — Francis Ford Coppola, starring Martin Sheen and Marlon Brando. The documentary "Hearts of Darkness" chronicles the production's mayhem. Brando arrived on set overweight and unprepared; Coppola had to shoot him in shadow from the shoulders up.

events.title: Jurassic Park Released
events.blurb: A 46-year-old director released an adaptation of a recent Michael Crichton novel about genetically resurrected dinosaurs on a tropical-island theme park. The film's digital dinosaurs — only a few minutes of CGI, mixed with extensive full-size animatronic puppets — changed the calculus of what visual effects could do. Audiences gasped at a Tyrannosaurus rex roaring over a rain-soaked jeep; a decade of purely physical-effects films were obsolete.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1993 — Steven Spielberg. The T. rex breaking into the jeep was actually animatronic; it malfunctioned often in the Hawaii humidity. The film displaced E.T. as highest-grossing ever. Spielberg was editing "Schindler's List" at night during production.

events.title: Sargon Founds the Akkadian Empire
events.blurb: A royal cupbearer of Mesopotamian origin, whose own infancy legends described a reed-basket journey down a river, overthrew his king and went on to subdue the patchwork of Sumerian city-states that had squabbled for centuries. He united them under a single administration that stretched from the Mediterranean coast to the Persian Gulf, establishing what is generally considered the first empire in human history.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2334 BCE — Sargon of Akkad. His dynasty lasted roughly 180 years before collapsing under external pressure. His granddaughter Enheduanna, high priestess at Ur, became the first named author in world literature. The famous "Mask of Sargon" bronze portrait is either him or a successor — ambiguous.

events.title: Battle of Cannae
events.blurb: Hannibal's army of roughly 50,000 men destroyed a Roman force of 80,000 in a single afternoon by letting the Roman center push forward into a concave line, then closing cavalry on both flanks until the entire legionary mass was encircled and butchered. Between 55,000 and 70,000 Romans died; senators threw handfuls of gold rings stripped from dead equestrians into a bowl to show Carthage the scale of the slaughter.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 216 BCE, Apulia. The double-envelopment Hannibal used at Cannae became the template studied at military academies for 2,000 years. Hannibal's war elephants, his most famous asset, had all died before this battle.

events.title: Julius Caesar Assassinated
events.blurb: A Roman dictator, having been named dictator-for-life a month earlier, was stabbed 23 times by a group of 60 senators at a meeting of the Senate held in a Pompey-built theatre. The assassins, styling themselves "Liberators," had convinced themselves that removing the man who had effectively ended the Republic would restore it. Instead, his death plunged Rome into 14 more years of civil war, at the end of which his adopted heir emerged as the first Roman emperor in all but name.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 44 BCE — the Ides of March. Conspirators included Brutus and Cassius. The supposed last words "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare; Caesar's actual last words — if he spoke any — may have been the Greek "kai su, teknon?" ("you too, my child?"). His heir Octavian defeated the conspirators at Philippi two years later.

events.title: Destruction of the Second Temple
events.blurb: A Roman general's army of 70,000 legionaries, closing the siege of a rebellious Judean capital after a four-year Jewish revolt, breached the walls and burned the city's Second Temple on the anniversary of the first Temple's destruction 656 years earlier. The Temple was never rebuilt; a Western retaining wall remains the holiest site in Judaism. Roman troops hauled the Temple menorah and other sacred vessels to Rome, where a victory arch depicting the procession still stands.
events.revealBlurb: 70 CE — the siege was commanded by Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian. The Arch of Titus, completed c. 81 CE, still stands at the east end of the Roman Forum. The Western Wall is the most significant surviving fragment; Orthodox Jews mourn the Temple's destruction each year on Tisha B'Av.

events.title: Hadrian's Wall Begun
events.blurb: A Roman emperor, touring his empire's northern frontier in Britannia, ordered the construction of a 117-kilometre stone-and-turf fortification across the narrow neck of the island from coast to coast. Sixteen forts and dozens of smaller milecastles were strung along it, garrisoned by auxiliary troops from across the empire. It was less a continuous fighting wall than a filter — controlling movement, collecting customs, and projecting imperial authority. Much of it still stands; the wall defined the political frontier for three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 122 CE — Emperor Hadrian. Construction took six years and employed three legions. Hadrian himself famously declared at the start of his reign that Rome would not continue to expand its borders indefinitely — reversing his predecessor Trajan's conquests in Mesopotamia.

events.title: First Spacewalk
events.blurb: Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov floated outside Voskhod 2 through an inflatable airlock and spent 12 minutes and 9 seconds in open space — the first human extravehicular activity. His spacesuit then ballooned in the vacuum to the point where he could no longer fit back through the hatch, forcing him to bleed pressure from a valve before squeezing inside headfirst.
events.revealBlurb: March 18, 1965 — Voskhod 2. The suit's engineers had fitted it with a built-in suicide pill. Leonov later said sweat filled his boots to the knee from the exertion of forcing himself back in. The spacecraft also drifted into an unplanned orbit and landed 386 km off target in the Ural mountains, where the crew spent a night in wolf country.

events.title: ISS First Crewed Occupation
events.blurb: A three-person crew docked a Soyuz capsule to the International Space Station's Zvezda module at 09:21 UTC, beginning a continuous human presence in low Earth orbit that has not been interrupted since. The station at that point consisted of three connected modules spanning roughly 27 meters, a fraction of its eventual 109-meter length.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 2000 — Expedition 1. Commander Bill Shepherd radioed NASA to request the station's call sign be changed from "Alpha" to "International Space Station" — a small act of diplomacy that stuck. The crew of two Russians and one American had access to less than 425 cubic meters of living space, about the volume of a large school bus.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Cassini Enters Saturn Orbit
events.blurb: The Cassini–Huygens spacecraft fired its main engine for 96 minutes to decelerate into Saturn orbit, threading a gap between the planet's F and G rings — a maneuver so precisely executed that the trajectory team reported it arrived within one kilometer of the planned position. Cassini became the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn, beginning a 13-year study of the planet and its moons.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 2004 — Cassini. Six months later, Cassini released the Huygens probe, which descended through Titan's atmosphere and transmitted data from its surface — the most distant landing ever achieved at the time. Cassini ultimately discovered that Enceladus has active geysers of water vapor, making it one of the top candidates for extraterrestrial life.

events.title: First South Pole Moon Landing
events.blurb: India's Chandrayaan-3 Vikram lander set down at 69°S latitude near the lunar south pole — the highest-latitude soft landing on the Moon ever achieved — just days after a Russian Luna-25 mission attempting the same target crashed on approach. The Pragyan rover confirmed the presence of sulfur, oxygen, iron, and other elements in the regolith through laser spectroscopy.
events.revealBlurb: August 23, 2023 — Chandrayaan-3. The mission cost approximately $75 million — cheaper than many Hollywood blockbusters and a fraction of comparable NASA missions. India became only the fourth nation to soft-land on the Moon and the first to reach the south polar region. The rover covered 100 meters before being placed in sleep mode ahead of the lunar night; it did not wake up.

events.title: Salt March Begins
events.blurb: A 60-year-old lawyer in a homespun loincloth set out from his ashram with 78 followers to walk 390 kilometres to the coast, intending to violate a colonial monopoly by picking up a pinch of seawater-evaporated salt. The 24-day trek grew into a procession of thousands; the defiance of the salt law spread across the country within weeks. 60,000 Indians, including the leader himself, were jailed within three months.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1930 — Gandhi begins the Dandi March from Sabarmati Ashram. Newspapers across the world carried photographs of him scooping up salt on the beach on April 6. Winston Churchill, watching from Westminster, privately described the prospect of "seditious middle-temple lawyer" meeting the viceroy as nauseating.

events.title: Bhagat Singh Executed
events.blurb: Three young revolutionaries were hanged an hour earlier than scheduled at a jail in a Punjabi city, after a three-year trial for killing a British police officer they had mistaken for the superintendent they had meant to assassinate. The youngest of them was 23. Crowds had gathered outside the prison expecting the normal morning execution time; by the time they arrived, the bodies had already been smuggled out and cremated by the riverside.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 1931 — Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev at Lahore Central Jail. Their martyrdom made them arguably the most venerated revolutionaries of the independence movement, an icon Gandhi's non-violent path never quite matched among the young.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Indo-Pakistani War of 1965
events.blurb: Infiltrators crossed the ceasefire line into a disputed northern territory to incite a rebellion that failed to materialize. India retaliated by invading across the international border toward a major Pakistani city. Seventeen days of conventional ground and air combat across the Punjab plains ended in stalemate, with each side convinced it had won. 3,000 Indian and 3,800 Pakistani soldiers died.
events.revealBlurb: August-September 1965 — ended by the Tashkent Declaration in January. The Battle of Asal Uttar saw one of the largest tank battles since WWII. Neither side's territorial changes amounted to much, and what they gained was returned at Tashkent.

events.title: Economic Liberalization
events.blurb: Facing a balance-of-payments crisis so acute that the country had airlifted 47 tonnes of its gold reserves to London as collateral, a new finance minister presented a budget that systematically dismantled the license-permit-quota economy that had governed Indian business for four decades. Industrial licensing was abolished, imports liberalized, foreign investment welcomed. The economy would nearly quintuple over the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 24, 1991 — Finance Minister Manmohan Singh's budget speech. Prime Minister Narasimha Rao provided the political cover. Singh, invoking Victor Hugo, declared: "No power on Earth can stop an idea whose time has come."

events.title: Pont du Gard Built
events.blurb: A three-tiered limestone aqueduct bridge was constructed to carry water 50 kilometres across southern Gaul to the Roman colony of Nemausus (modern Nîmes). The top level — 48 metres above the River Gard — still carried its channel; the whole structure spans 275 metres. It was built dry, without mortar, using stones so precisely cut that the joints remain watertight after two millennia. The aqueduct itself was decommissioned in the 6th century; the bridge survived as a road crossing.
events.revealBlurb: c. 50 CE — built under Emperor Claudius. The water it carried had a gradient of only 1 in 3,000 — about 30 centimetres of drop per kilometre. The Pont du Gard is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited tourist destinations in France.

events.title: Angkor Wat Completed
events.blurb: A Khmer king completed a vast temple complex in his capital, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and later converted to Buddhist use. Covering over 160 hectares, surrounded by a moat, topped with a central tower 65 metres high, and decorated with 1.6 kilometres of bas-relief carvings illustrating Hindu epics, it was the largest religious monument in the world. After the Khmer capital shifted in the 15th century, the jungle gradually overgrew the complex, which was rediscovered by European travellers in the 19th century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1150 — King Suryavarman II, in the capital of the Khmer Empire (modern Cambodia). It appears on the Cambodian flag — the only national flag featuring a building. French explorer Henri Mouhot's 1861 account brought it to Western attention, though it had never actually been "lost."

events.title: Sagrada Família Begun
events.blurb: Construction began on a Catholic basilica in the Catalan capital, funded by donations alone — a condition that would stretch the project across a century and a half. The original architect was replaced after one year by a 31-year-old ferociously religious designer who would pour the rest of his life into the project, combining Gothic and Art Nouveau influences into a style of his own. He would die 43 years later, hit by a tram on the street outside; only a fraction of the church was finished. Construction continues today.
events.revealBlurb: March 19, 1882 — original architect Francisco de Paula del Villar; succeeded 1883 by Antoni Gaudí. Gaudí devoted the last 15 years of his life exclusively to the project. He was hit by a tram on June 7, 1926; his grave is in the crypt. Completion is projected for 2026 — a century after his death.

events.title: Statue of Liberty Dedicated
events.blurb: A 46-metre-tall copper statue of a robed woman holding a torch, a gift from the French people commemorating American independence (with an eye toward French republican aspirations), was dedicated on a small island in New York Harbor in the rain. It had been designed by a French sculptor, its internal iron framework engineered by the man who would five years later design a certain Paris tower, and shipped across the Atlantic in 350 pieces.
events.revealBlurb: October 28, 1886 — sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi; engineer Gustave Eiffel. The statue was meant to arrive for the 1876 centennial; it missed by a decade due to fundraising troubles. The poem on its pedestal ("Give me your tired, your poor...") was added in 1903 from a sonnet by Emma Lazarus.

events.title: Channel Tunnel Opens
events.blurb: A 50-kilometre twin-bore railway tunnel under the English Channel opened, linking France to Britain below the sea floor for the first time in 8,000 years. The tunnel had been proposed repeatedly since the early 19th century but had always been shelved on defensive grounds; the end of the Cold War and European integration finally made it buildable. Construction had involved eleven tunnel-boring machines drilling simultaneously from both sides; the breakthrough was within 35 centimetres alignment.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1994 — Queen Elizabeth II and President François Mitterrand cut a ribbon jointly. Total project cost: £9 billion, roughly 80 percent over budget. The tunnel is used by Eurostar passenger trains and the freight-carrying Shuttle. Trains reach 160 km/h underground.

events.title: Giotto's Arena Chapel Frescoes
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a fresco cycle covering the interior walls of a small private chapel in a northern Italian city, commissioned by a banker trying to atone for his father's usury. The artist's naturalistic figures, three-dimensional space, and emotional humanism broke decisively with Byzantine conventions and set the visual vocabulary of the next three centuries. Vasari would later date the start of the Renaissance from his work.
events.revealBlurb: 1305 — Giotto di Bondone, at the Scrovegni (Arena) Chapel in Padua. Enrico Scrovegni built the chapel on the site of a Roman arena, and commissioned the frescoes to atone for the soul of his father, named in Dante's Inferno.

events.title: Botticelli's Primavera
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a large poplar panel for the bedroom of a Medici cousin, depicting nine mythological figures in a grove of orange trees — Venus at the centre, the Three Graces dancing, a gusting wind god chasing a nymph who is transformed into the flower-bearing goddess of spring. It is among the first Renaissance paintings to take mythological (not religious) subject matter on its own terms.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1482 — Sandro Botticelli. The painting contains at least 500 identifiable plant species, some 190 different flowers. Botticelli was later nearly destroyed by Savonarola's movement and reportedly burned some of his own work in the bonfire of the vanities.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Caravaggio's Calling of St Matthew
events.blurb: A 28-year-old painter completed the first of three monumental canvases for a chapel in a Roman church, depicting the moment when Christ walks into a tax collector's office and wordlessly summons a clerk to follow him. A shaft of natural light cuts diagonally across the scene, picking out faces from deep shadow. The painter used Roman street-people as models and dressed the apostles in contemporary clothes. The effect shocked and recruited a generation of imitators across Europe.
events.revealBlurb: 1600 — Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio, at the Contarelli Chapel, San Luigi dei Francesi. Art historians still argue about which figure is Matthew. The painter killed a man in a brawl six years later and died on the run at 38.

events.title: Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring
events.blurb: A Dutch painter in his early thirties completed an intimate oil study on canvas of a young woman turning toward the viewer, her head covered in a blue and yellow turban, a single teardrop-shaped pearl catching the light at her ear. It was not a commissioned portrait but a "tronie" — a character study. The artist made only about 35 paintings in his career; this one was rediscovered in 1881 at auction for two guilders.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1665 — Johannes Vermeer. Now in the Mauritshuis in The Hague. The "pearl" may actually be tin or glass — no pearl of that size is plausible. Tracy Chevalier's 1999 novel and the 2003 film made it a pop-culture icon.

events.title: Luther Posts the 95 Theses
events.blurb: A 33-year-old German university theologian sent his local archbishop a letter enclosing a 95-point list of academic propositions challenging the papal indulgence system — the practice of selling forgiveness of sins. By tradition, he also posted the Latin theses on the door of his university church, which served as a community bulletin board. Copies reached print within weeks and spread across Germany. He had intended academic debate; he ignited the Protestant Reformation.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1517 — Martin Luther at Wittenberg Castle Church. Most scholars doubt the physical nailing-to-the-door story; the letter to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz is well-documented. October 31 is now celebrated as Reformation Day in many Protestant countries.

events.title: Magellan's Fleet Departs
events.blurb: Five ships and 270 sailors departed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda under a Portuguese navigator flying a Spanish flag, carrying provisions for two years. Three years later, one battered ship and 18 survivors returned — the first vessels to circumnavigate the globe, though their commander had been killed in a Filipino skirmish partway through.

events.title: Henry VIII Breaks with Rome
events.blurb: An English parliament passed an Act of Supremacy declaring the king — who had wanted for years to annul his marriage to a Spanish princess who had given him no male heir, and whom the pope had refused — the "Supreme Head" of the Church of England. The break with Rome was not primarily theological; the king remained Catholic in doctrine for the rest of his life. It rewrote England's religious, political, and property landscape for the next century.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1534 — Henry VIII. He had already married Anne Boleyn (his second wife) in secret in January 1533. The archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Cranmer, had annulled his first marriage in May. Henry would have six wives; two were beheaded, two divorced, one died in childbirth.

events.title: Globe Theatre Opens
events.blurb: A London acting company, evicted from their original playhouse when their landlord refused to renew the lease, dismantled the building overnight, carried the timbers across the frozen Thames, and rebuilt them into a new circular theatre on the south bank. Their principal playwright and shareholder produced several of his greatest plays on its stage over the next 14 years, until a cannon effect during a performance of Henry VIII set the thatched roof alight.
events.revealBlurb: 1599 — the Lord Chamberlain's Men; William Shakespeare was a shareholder. It burned on June 29, 1613; was rebuilt; was demolished in 1644 under Puritan hostility to theatre. A faithful replica opened in 1997 near the original site.

events.title: Dutch East India Company Founded
events.blurb: The Dutch government chartered a joint-stock corporation with a 21-year monopoly on Asian trade, the authority to wage war, build forts, coin money, and conclude treaties in the name of the States General. It was the world's first publicly traded multinational corporation. Within decades it dominated the Asian spice trade, conquered chunks of Southeast Asia, and declared its own wars. At its height its market capitalization exceeded that of the combined top ten companies of today.
events.revealBlurb: March 20, 1602 — Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC). It employed over 70,000 people at its peak. Its share price rose 1,200 percent in the 1600s and collapsed in 1799 when the company was bankrupted by corruption, wars, and changing trade patterns.

events.title: Intel 4004 Microprocessor Released
events.blurb: Intel released a 4-bit central processing unit containing 2,300 transistors on a silicon chip the size of a fingernail, capable of 60,000 operations per second. Originally designed for a Japanese calculator company, it became the world's first commercially available microprocessor — the prototype for every CPU that followed.

events.title: IBM Personal Computer Launched
events.blurb: A technology corporation released a personal computer based on an Intel processor running an operating system licensed from a small software company for $25,000. Its open architecture allowed third-party manufacturers to build compatible clones, spawning a global personal computer industry worth trillions within a decade.

events.title: Intel Pentium Released
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley chipmaker released the fifth generation of its mass-market microprocessor under the brand name "Pentium" — a word coined to be trademarkable, since numerical names like "586" were not. The chip included 3.1 million transistors and outperformed its 486 predecessor by a factor of two. A subtle floating-point division bug discovered by a math professor the following year forced a $475 million recall.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1993 — Intel Pentium (P5). The floating-point bug (the FDIV bug) was discovered by Thomas Nicely of Lynchburg College. Initially Intel offered replacements only to customers who could prove they used the chip for heavy math. Bad PR forced full replacement.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: AlphaGo Beats Lee Sedol
events.blurb: A London-based artificial intelligence laboratory's go-playing program, trained on millions of human games and then on games it had played against itself, defeated the reigning world champion of the ancient Asian board game 4–1 in a five-game match in Seoul. The match was broadcast live to 280 million people. Experts had predicted a champion-beating go program was a decade away; the algorithmic gap between games like chess and go had seemed insurmountable.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 2016 — DeepMind's AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol. Lee's single winning game, move 78 — the "divine move" — exploited a subtle blind spot in the AI. DeepMind was acquired by Google in 2014 for around $500 million. Lee retired from professional go three years later, partly because AI had changed the game.

events.title: Battle of Britain
events.blurb: For nearly four months, an island nation's outnumbered fighter force faced daily mass raids by the world's most battle-hardened air force, with the explicit goal of destroying aerial defences so that a seaborne invasion could follow. Radar stations, sector control rooms, and the pilots' ability to keep flying became the three fulcrums on which the outcome balanced.
events.revealBlurb: July 10 – October 31, 1940. The RAF lost 1,023 aircraft; the Luftwaffe lost 1,887. Churchill's "The Few" speech on August 20 honoured the pilots — the average age of whom was just 20. Germany quietly postponed its invasion plan on September 17 and never rescheduled it.

events.title: Me 262's First All-Jet Flight
events.blurb: A swept-wing aircraft climbed away from a Bavarian airfield under pure jet power for the first time, reaching speeds that no piston-engined fighter could match, signalling that the era of propeller-driven military aviation was ending. The technology was real and available — but bureaucratic delays and a leadership obsession with bombers kept it from operational service for more than two years.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 1942, Leipheim — pilot Fritz Wendel flew the Me 262 V3 on jet power alone for the first time. Hitler later insisted the aircraft be developed as a bomber rather than a fighter, reportedly costing Germany a 14-month delay. When it finally entered service in 1944, it was too little too late: fuel shortages kept most on the ground.

events.title: Birkenau Gas Chambers Operational
