events.blurb: Four large purpose-built structures combining undressing rooms, sealed chambers, and industrial crematoria were completed and put into continuous operation at a camp in occupied Poland, creating a killing capacity of several thousand people per day and establishing the industrial infrastructure used to murder the majority of the Holocaust's victims.
events.revealBlurb: The four large crematoria-gas chamber complexes at Auschwitz-Birkenau came fully operational between March and June 1943. At peak operation in the summer of 1944, during the deportation of Hungarian Jews, they killed and cremated up to 10,000 people per day. The Sonderkommando — prisoner workers forced to operate the crematoria — later buried written testimony in the ash.

events.title: Battle of Okinawa
events.blurb: 180,000 American troops landed on an island 350 miles from the Japanese home islands on Easter Sunday, triggering the largest amphibious assault in the Pacific and the longest land battle of that theatre — 82 days of cave-to-cave fighting, mass suicide charges, and the heaviest naval losses the United States suffered in any single campaign.
events.revealBlurb: April 1 – June 22, 1945. US casualties: roughly 12,000 killed and 36,000 wounded. Japanese military deaths: over 110,000. An estimated 100,000 Okinawan civilians also died. The kamikaze campaign sank 36 US ships and damaged 368. American planners, projecting similar resistance during a home-island invasion, estimated 1 million US casualties — a figure that influenced the decision to use atomic bombs.

events.title: Execution of Mussolini
events.blurb: The founder of one of the 20th century's major fascist movements was captured hiding in a German military convoy while attempting to flee across a northern border, taken to a lakeside village by communist partisans, and shot 26 hours later — his body then transported to a major city and hung upside down at a petrol station for public display.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 1945 — executed at Giulino di Mezzegra on Lake Como, two days before Hitler's death. Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci were shot, then driven to Milan and strung up by their heels at the Piazzale Loreto — the same square where partisan hostages had been publicly displayed by Fascists a year earlier.

events.title: Third Dynasty of Ur Founded
events.blurb: A king named Ur-Namma united Mesopotamia after a period of fragmentation and built its most iconic religious structures — stepped pyramid-temples called ziggurats — in every major city. He also issued the oldest surviving law code in history, predating the more famous Babylonian one by three centuries. His successor standardized weights, measures, and the calendar across the entire empire, and administered it through a vast network of clay-tablet bureaucracy.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2112 BCE — Ur, Mesopotamia. Ur-Namma founded the dynasty; his son Shulgi ran it for 48 years with remarkable administrative efficiency. The ziggurat of Ur, built for the moon god Nanna, still stands 30 metres high today — one of the best-preserved structures from the ancient Near East.

events.title: Phoenician Alphabet Comes Into Use
events.blurb: Merchants and scribes along the eastern Mediterranean coast standardized a writing system using 22 consonant letters — the first alphabet with a fixed right-to-left writing direction. The system required no specialist training to learn and could be adapted to write almost any spoken language. It spread rapidly through sea trade to Greece, where vowel letters were added, producing the ancestor of every modern European alphabet.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1050 BCE — Levantine coast (modern Lebanon). The Phoenician alphabet evolved from earlier Proto-Canaanite scripts. The oldest securely dated inscription is on a bronze arrowhead from around 1000 BCE. Within three centuries, adapted versions of this script would be writing Greek, Aramaic, Hebrew, and Arabic.

events.title: Fall of Nineveh
events.blurb: A coalition army besieged the largest city in the world for three months before breaking through its walls in August and systematically burning the palaces and temples within. The city, which had served as capital of a state that controlled Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Levant simultaneously, was so thoroughly destroyed that a Greek historian would write of it two centuries later without knowing where it had stood. The king defending the city died in the sack.
events.revealBlurb: August 612 BCE — Nineveh (modern Mosul, Iraq). The coalition was led by the Neo-Babylonian king Nabopolassar and the Median king Cyaxares. The burning of the palace accidentally fired the clay tablets in Ashurbanipal's library, preserving them. The city was not fully abandoned until the 7th century CE.

events.title: Library of Alexandria Established
events.blurb: A Macedonian king's scholarly advisor was charged with assembling a universal library in the new capital city — a building intended to collect every text ever written, in every language. Ships arriving in the harbor were searched for scrolls, which were confiscated, copied, and returned. The institution was attached to a research center called the Mouseion where scholars in medicine, mathematics, astronomy, and literature received royal stipends to work full-time.
events.revealBlurb: c. 295 BCE — Alexandria, Egypt. Conceived by Ptolemy I; built under Ptolemy II. Demetrius of Phalerum, an Athenian philosopher, was the founding librarian. The library eventually held an estimated 400,000–700,000 scrolls. It did not burn in a single dramatic fire — it declined gradually over centuries.

events.title: Rosetta Stone Decree Issued
events.blurb: A congress of priests convened at Memphis to celebrate a royal coronation and issued a decree granting temple tax exemptions, priestly stipend increases, prisoner amnesty, and renewed support for sacred animal cults. The decree was engraved in two forms of Egyptian script and in Greek onto a granodiorite stele and distributed to temples across the country. The king in whose honor it was issued was thirteen years old.
events.revealBlurb: March 27, 196 BCE — Memphis, Egypt. Ptolemy V Epiphanes. The stele was later carried off by French soldiers in 1799, surrendered to the British, and now sits in the British Museum. Champollion used it in 1822 to crack Egyptian hieroglyphics.

events.title: Hippocratic Oath Composed
events.blurb: Greek medical writers associated with a physician teaching on an Aegean island composed a short ethical oath addressed to Apollo and Asclepius, binding physicians to care for their patients, respect their teachers, preserve patient confidences, and do no harm. The document is arguably the oldest surviving code of professional ethics. Modern versions, substantially modified, are still sworn by many medical-school graduates.
events.revealBlurb: c. 400 BCE — attributed to Hippocrates of Kos, though probably composed by his students or school. The modern "first, do no harm" is actually not in the original Greek text; it appears later in Hippocrates' Epidemics. The oath still shows up at white-coat ceremonies.

events.title: Jenner's First Vaccination
events.blurb: A 47-year-old English country doctor in Gloucestershire inoculated an 8-year-old boy with pus scraped from the hand of a milkmaid who had contracted cowpox, a mild disease related to smallpox but harmless in humans. Six weeks later he inoculated the boy with actual smallpox. The boy did not get sick. The doctor wrote up his results, which transformed public health across the world over the next two centuries.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1796 — Edward Jenner inoculated James Phipps. The word "vaccine" comes from vacca (Latin for cow). Jenner refused to patent the procedure despite the enormous potential fortune, insisting it was a gift to humanity. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 — the only disease eliminated through vaccination.

events.title: Koch Identifies TB Bacillus
events.blurb: A 38-year-old German physician, presenting to the Berlin Physiological Society, announced he had isolated and cultured the bacillus responsible for tuberculosis — a disease that killed roughly one in seven people in 19th-century Europe. He had developed systematic protocols — now called Koch's postulates — for identifying which microbes caused which diseases. He would identify the cholera bacillus two years later.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1882 — Robert Koch. World Tuberculosis Day is commemorated on this anniversary each year. Koch won the Nobel Prize in 1905. His attempted TB vaccine, tuberculin, was a failure — but became a useful skin test for TB exposure.

events.title: Röntgen Discovers X-Rays
events.blurb: A 50-year-old German physicist, working with a cathode-ray tube covered in black cardboard, noticed that a paper screen coated in barium platinocyanide glowed even when placed some distance away. He realized the tube was emitting an invisible, unknown type of radiation. Further experiments showed the rays penetrated paper, wood, aluminum, and even human flesh — but not bone. He published an image of his wife's hand, showing her skeleton and wedding ring.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1895 — Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen at the University of Würzburg. He called the phenomenon "X" rays because he didn't know what they were. He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. The image of his wife's hand, published in early 1896, is arguably the first diagnostic X-ray.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: CNN Launches
events.blurb: A 24-hour cable news network began broadcasting from a converted country-club headquarters in a southeastern U.S. city, defying widespread industry skepticism that there was enough daily news to fill a full day of programming. The network's first broadcast began with its founder and his wife standing in front of an American flag. Its approach — continuous live coverage, rolling updates, no fixed broadcast schedule — eventually reshaped how all news was delivered.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1980 — Ted Turner's Cable News Network, Atlanta. The Gulf War coverage in 1991, broadcast live from Baghdad as bombs fell, established CNN's dominance. Turner had filmed a doomsday video, intended to play only at the literal end of the world, saying farewell to viewers.

events.title: Prince Charles Marries Diana
events.blurb: The heir to the British throne, 32, married a 20-year-old shy nursery-school assistant at a grand ceremony at a London cathedral. The televised wedding drew 750 million viewers worldwide and unfolded like a fairytale: horse-drawn carriages, a 25-foot train on the bride's silk ivory dress, a balcony kiss at a royal palace afterward. The marriage itself would be miserable; the couple separated in 1992 and divorced in 1996. Both remarried others, and the bride died in a Paris car crash in 1997.
events.revealBlurb: July 29, 1981 — Charles, Prince of Wales and Lady Diana Spencer at St. Paul's Cathedral. Diana tripped on her father's name during the vows ("Philip Charles Arthur George" instead of "Charles Philip..."). Charles, now King Charles III, succeeded his mother Elizabeth II in September 2022.

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: South Park Premieres
events.blurb: An animated half-hour adult-comedy series about four foul-mouthed 8-year-old boys in a small Colorado mountain town premiered on the Comedy Central cable network. The deliberately crude cut-paper animation style and its topical-to-the-minute production timeline (each episode was produced in a week rather than the months typical for animation) gave it a reactive speed no other animated show could match. It would remain in production for over 25 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1997 — created by Trey Parker and Matt Stone. Their earlier Christmas short, "The Spirit of Christmas," had circulated as a VHS among Hollywood executives in 1995. The show's 1999 feature film nearly received an NC-17 rating; the MPAA gave it R after the creators submitted it six times.

events.title: Seinfeld Finale
events.blurb: The 180th and final episode of a nine-year NBC sitcom about petty New York narcissists aired to 76 million viewers. The divisive finale had the four main characters put on trial in a fictional Massachusetts town for failing to help a carjacking victim, watched by a parade of minor characters from earlier seasons who had been wronged by them. Critics and fans were largely disappointed; its creator defended it as consistent with the show's amoral premise.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1998 — "The Finale." Written by Larry David, returning after leaving the show in 1996. Ad slots on the finale sold for around $2 million for 30 seconds — a pre-Super Bowl record for a TV program.

events.title: First World Series
events.blurb: A best-of-nine championship series between the American League and National League pennant winners was played — the first time the two major leagues had agreed to a postseason championship after years of cold war. An underdog American League team, the Boston Americans, defeated the heavily favoured Pittsburgh Pirates 5 games to 3. The Pirates' owner, Barney Dreyfuss, had proposed the series himself.
events.revealBlurb: October 1-13, 1903 — Boston Americans (later the Red Sox) beat the Pittsburgh Pirates. Cy Young, Boston's 36-year-old ace, started game 3 but was the losing pitcher. Dreyfuss gave his losing Pirates a share of the winners' purse to compensate. No World Series was held in 1904; it became annual from 1905.

events.title: Bannister's 4-Minute Mile
events.blurb: A 25-year-old medical student in his final year of training, racing on a windy Oxford track in a university-versus-amateur competition, ran a mile in 3 minutes and 59.4 seconds — the first human ever to break the four-minute barrier. The record stood for 46 days. His pacers, who trailed off at the halfway and three-quarter marks on a pre-arranged plan, were athletes the newspapers had not noticed. Sport doctors had warned a sub-four mile might be physiologically impossible.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1954 — Roger Bannister at Iffley Road track. Pacers: Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway. John Landy of Australia broke Bannister's record 46 days later. Bannister beat him in the "Mile of the Century" race at the Vancouver Commonwealth Games in August 1954 — both running sub-four.

events.title: Pelé Wins First World Cup
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Brazilian forward, playing in his first senior international tournament, scored two goals in the World Cup final as Brazil beat the host nation 5-2 to win football's greatest prize for the first time in the country's history. He became the youngest player ever to score in a World Cup final; his performance vaulted Brazilian football onto the world stage. He would go on to win two more World Cups over the following 12 years.
events.revealBlurb: June 29, 1958 — Pelé (Edson Arantes do Nascimento) at the Råsunda Stadium, Solna, Sweden. Brazil 5, Sweden 2. Pelé was carried off the field by his teammates at the end. He remains the only player to win three World Cups.

events.title: India Wins Cricket World Cup
events.blurb: The Indian men's cricket team won their second-ever Cricket World Cup, beating Sri Lanka by six wickets in the final at a Mumbai stadium in front of a home crowd that included the country's most beloved cricketer, who was playing in his sixth and final World Cup. The tournament winner's 36-year-old captain carried the little master on his shoulders around the stadium in celebration. It was the first time any nation had won a World Cup final on its own soil.
events.revealBlurb: April 2, 2011 — India beat Sri Lanka at Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai. Captain MS Dhoni hit the winning six. Sachin Tendulkar's 28 runs in his final-ever ODI innings on the way to the trophy saw him carried on teammates' shoulders around the stadium.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Paradise Lost Published
events.blurb: A blind 58-year-old English poet, dictating to a rotating cast of scribes, completed a 10-book (later 12-book) epic poem retelling the Biblical account of the fall of man from the perspective of a sympathetically characterized Satan. Having narrowly escaped execution for his political writings under the restored monarchy, he was paid ten pounds for the manuscript. It would become the template for English epic poetry.
events.revealBlurb: 1667 — John Milton. He had gone blind in 1652 from untreated glaucoma. His daughters had to be taught to read — including Hebrew, Greek, and Latin — just so they could transcribe his dictations. "The mind is its own place..." is from Book I.

events.title: Johnson's Dictionary Published
events.blurb: An Oxford-educated English essayist, working nine years with six assistants in a garret flat, completed and published a two-volume dictionary of the English language — the first comprehensive, systematically illustrated dictionary of the vernacular. It defined 42,773 words with 114,000 quotations showing their use. It was the standard English dictionary until Oxford's larger project finally superseded it 173 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1755 — Samuel Johnson. He defined "lexicographer" as "a harmless drudge, that busies himself in tracing the original, and detailing the signification of words." His tart definitions became famous in their own right: "Oats: A grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people."

events.title: Leaves of Grass Published
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Brooklyn printer, essayist, and newspaper editor self-published a small quarto of 12 unrhymed, unmetered poems celebrating the American body politic in a language saturated with sexual frankness. It drew praise from Ralph Waldo Emerson and denunciation from almost everyone else. The author kept expanding and revising the volume for the rest of his life; the final 1892 "deathbed edition" contained over 400 poems.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1855 — Walt Whitman, self-published because no publisher would take it. He set much of it himself at a Brooklyn print shop. His job at the Department of the Interior was terminated in 1865 after the Secretary read a copy and called it obscene.

events.title: Les Misérables Published
events.blurb: A 60-year-old French novelist living in exile on the Channel Island of Guernsey published a 1,500-page five-volume novel tracing the arc of a paroled convict redeeming himself over decades, set against the 1832 June Rebellion in Paris. He had been working on it, off and on, for seventeen years. The publisher sent the first volume simultaneously to seven European capitals; the author paid for advertising out of his own pocket. It was an instant international sensation.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 1862 — Victor Hugo. The famous shortest correspondence in literary history happened around this book: Hugo, on holiday, wired his publisher "?" — the reply came back "!" — confirming strong sales.

events.title: To Kill a Mockingbird Published
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Alabama-born New York airline reservation clerk published her first and, for over half a century, only novel — a semi-autobiographical story narrated by a six-year-old white girl whose father, a small-town Southern lawyer, defends a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman. The book won a Pulitzer the next year and has been a school-curriculum fixture in the U.S. ever since.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 1960 — Harper Lee. Her childhood friend Truman Capote was the model for the character Dill. Gregory Peck won an Oscar for the film adaptation. Lee published a second novel, "Go Set a Watchman," in 2015, a year before her death; it was an earlier draft of the same book.

events.title: Cartwright Patents Power Loom
events.blurb: A 42-year-old Anglican clergyman with no mechanical training, visiting a Derbyshire cotton mill, was so struck by the mismatch between fast-spinning machinery and hand weaving that he went home and built a water-powered weaving loom. His early designs barely worked, but subsequent refinements by others made mechanical weaving commercially viable by the 1820s and obsolete the ancient hand-loom trade. Hundreds of thousands of English and Indian weavers lost their livelihoods.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1785 — Edmund Cartwright. His brother had predicted that Arkwright's spinning machines would flood the market with yarn that hand-weavers could not process; the power loom was his answer. His own mill burned down twice, possibly by angered hand-weavers.

events.title: Great Exhibition Opens
events.blurb: Queen Victoria opened a five-month international exhibition of industrial and artistic products housed in a vast prefabricated iron-and-glass structure in Hyde Park — the building nicknamed the "Crystal Palace." 14,000 exhibitors from 25 countries displayed 100,000 exhibits; six million visitors paid admission. The exhibition's organizer, Prince Albert, had intended it as both a celebration of industrial progress and a showcase for the superiority of free trade. It made a healthy profit, used to found London museums.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1851 — Prince Albert's Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations. Designer Joseph Paxton, a gardener turned architect, had designed the building in a single afternoon on a sheet of blotting paper. The profit funded the Victoria and Albert, Science, and Natural History museums.

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Ford Model T Goes on Sale
events.blurb: An American automaker released a new car designed to be cheap, simple to drive, and reliable on the rutted rural roads of the era. It sold for $850 — about half the price of the cheapest competitor. Over 19 years of production, the company would build 15 million of them, mostly painted black because that paint dried fastest. At peak production, a completed Model T rolled off the line every 24 seconds.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1908 — Ford Motor Company. The 1913-1914 introduction of the moving assembly line cut the Model T's price to $490. Henry Ford doubled the minimum wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day in January 1914, partly to cut turnover caused by the line's brutal monotony.

events.title: Terracotta Army Created
events.blurb: In a pit 1.5 kilometres east of the tomb of a Chinese emperor who had just died, labourers arranged some 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers, 130 chariots, and 670 horses facing east, ready to defend him in the afterlife. Each soldier's face was modelled individually; no two are identical. The figures had originally been painted in bright colours that flaked off within days of excavation when exposed to dry modern air.
events.revealBlurb: c. 210 BCE — the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of unified China. Rediscovered by local farmers drilling a well in March 1974. The emperor's own tomb mound remains unexcavated — ancient sources describe rivers of mercury; soil tests confirm unusual mercury levels.

events.title: Goya's Third of May 1808
events.blurb: A Spanish court painter in his late sixties completed a large canvas commemorating the execution of Spanish civilians by French occupying troops six years earlier. A man in a white shirt stretches his arms out cruciform, illuminated by a lantern at ground level; the executioners are faceless soldiers. The painting broke with the flattering conventions of history painting, depicting the victims as ordinary and terrified rather than heroic. Its brutality shocked its first audiences.
events.revealBlurb: 1814 — Francisco Goya. Commissioned, remarkably, by the restored Spanish monarch who the French had deposed — Ferdinand VII. Now in Madrid's Prado. It directly influenced Manet's Execution of Maximilian and Picasso's Guernica.

events.title: Hokusai's Great Wave
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Japanese printmaker produced the first of thirty-six woodblock prints depicting views of a sacred mountain, all showing it from different perspectives and in different weather. The first print, which viewers sometimes mistook for the title piece, showed an enormous wave curling in threatening foam over three small fishing boats, with the mountain a distant cone between its spray. The distinctive blue pigment, Prussian blue, was a recent European import.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1831 — Katsushika Hokusai. The print is one of the most widely reproduced images in the world; thousands of impressions survive. Hokusai called himself "the old man mad about drawing" and claimed he would become a true artist only at 110.

events.title: Armory Show Opens
events.blurb: An exhibition at a New York National Guard armory introduced American audiences to European modernism at industrial scale — 1,300 paintings and sculptures by artists most had never heard of, including Matisse, Picasso, Duchamp, and Brancusi. Duchamp's "Nude Descending a Staircase No. 2" was ridiculed by a popular cartoonist as "explosion in a shingle factory" and drew crowds for exactly that reason. The show moved on to Chicago and Boston and is credited with changing the course of American art.
events.revealBlurb: February 17 to March 15, 1913 — the 69th Regiment Armory, Lexington Avenue, NYC. Around 90,000 people visited in New York alone. Theodore Roosevelt wrote a mostly-baffled review; a reproduction of the "Nude" was burned in effigy at the Chicago Art Institute.

events.title: Pollock's Drip Paintings
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American painter, working in a converted barn studio on Long Island, laid large unstretched canvases on the floor and moved around their edges pouring and flinging paint from sticks and hardened brushes. The resulting "drip paintings" rejected representational composition entirely in favour of overall visual rhythm. A 1949 Life magazine spread asked: "Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?" and made him instantly famous and nearly famously alcoholic.
events.revealBlurb: 1947 — Jackson Pollock began the drip technique in Springs, NY. He died in a car crash driving drunk on August 11, 1956, aged 44. His "No. 5, 1948" sold privately in 2006 for $140 million, briefly the highest price ever paid for a painting.

events.title: NATO Founded
events.blurb: Twelve nations from both sides of the Atlantic signed a mutual defense treaty in Washington, D.C., committing that an armed attack against one would be considered an attack against all. The alliance was built around Article 5 — a collective defense clause that has been invoked exactly once in its history, after 9/11.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1949 — founding members included the US, UK, France, Canada, and eight others. Lord Ismay, its first Secretary General, quipped its purpose was "to keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down."

events.title: First Soviet Atomic Bomb Test
events.blurb: Four years after U.S. weapons ended the Pacific war, Soviet scientists detonated their own plutonium implosion device at a test range in the Kazakh steppe. Western intelligence had predicted the breakthrough was at least five years away. The explosion ended the American nuclear monopoly and opened the arms race.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 1949 — codename RDS-1, nicknamed "First Lightning." The design was largely cribbed from the U.S. Fat Man bomb via spy networks inside the Manhattan Project. Klaus Fuchs had handed over detailed blueprints.

events.title: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg Executed
events.blurb: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed by electric chair at Sing Sing Prison, having been convicted of passing atomic bomb design secrets to the Soviet Union — making them the only American civilians executed for espionage during the Cold War. Their case divided the nation, with their guilt debated in editorial pages, union halls, and diplomatic cables around the world.
events.revealBlurb: June 19, 1953 — Ossining, New York. Ethel Rosenberg required three jolts of electricity before she died; Julius was pronounced dead after the first. Subsequent release of Soviet archives confirmed Julius was a spy; historians still debate the extent of Ethel's involvement.

events.title: Prague Spring Invasion
events.blurb: Reform-minded leaders in a central European capital had spent eight months experimenting with "socialism with a human face" — easing censorship, rehabilitating purge victims, and tolerating debate. In the night, 250,000 Warsaw Pact soldiers and 2,000 tanks rolled across the borders. Unarmed civilians tried to argue with the invading soldiers; within days the reforms were reversed.
events.revealBlurb: August 20-21, 1968 — invasion of Czechoslovakia. Reformist leader Alexander Dubček was flown to Moscow and forced to sign a capitulation. A student named Jan Palach set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square five months later in protest.

events.title: Berlin Wall Falls
events.blurb: An East German government spokesman announced at a press conference that citizens could cross the border immediately, triggering jubilant crowds who arrived at checkpoints and began dismantling the 155-kilometre concrete barrier with hammers and their bare hands. More than two million East Germans crossed into West Berlin during the following weekend alone.

events.title: The Jazz Singer Released
events.blurb: A Warner Brothers feature film about a cantor's son who runs away to become a vaudeville singer premiered at a Times Square theatre as the first full-length motion picture with synchronized recorded dialogue. The star, in blackface for most of the film, delivered the industry's first-ever spoken movie line: "Wait a minute, wait a minute. You ain't heard nothin' yet!" Within three years almost every Hollywood film was a talkie.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1927 — Al Jolson at the Warners' Theatre, NYC. The film's sound system, Vitaphone, used synchronized phonograph records rather than optical audio. The silent era ended astonishingly fast; by 1930 the major Hollywood studios had written off the previous decade's technology.

events.title: First Academy Awards
events.blurb: A 15-minute banquet at a Hollywood hotel awarded twelve statuettes — a 34 cm tall gilded figure of a knight standing on a reel of film — to films, actors, directors, and technicians selected by the newly formed Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. 270 people attended. The winners had been announced three months earlier. The whole ceremony received brief mention in the next day's Los Angeles Times, on page 10.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 1929 — Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel. First Best Picture: "Wings." Best Actor: Emil Jannings. The bronze statuette's nickname, "Oscar," was supposedly coined by an Academy librarian who thought it resembled her Uncle Oscar; the story is almost certainly retrofitted.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey Released
events.blurb: A 39-year-old New York-born director released a 149-minute science-fiction film about human evolution, artificial intelligence, and alien contact, with minimal dialogue, a four-movement structure, and long classical-music sequences of spacecraft slowly docking to the Blue Danube. The first audience walked out in droves; reviews were mixed. Within two years, it was the highest-grossing film of its year and had reshaped what cinema was permitted to do.
events.revealBlurb: April 2, 1968 — Stanley Kubrick. Co-written with Arthur C. Clarke. The jump cut from a primeval bone thrown into the air to a spaceship in orbit covers 4 million years in one frame. HAL 9000's voice was performed by Canadian Shakespearean actor Douglas Rain.

events.title: The Matrix Released
events.blurb: Two siblings who had directed only one feature between them released a 136-minute science-fiction film in which the world turns out to be a computer simulation and humanity is harvested by machines as a power source. The film's "bullet time" effect — a camera arcing around a frozen-mid-action character while the world resumed behind it — became an instantly iconic technique. Its cyberpunk philosophy, couture, and green-tinted aesthetic defined the turn of the millennium.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1999 — Lana and Lilly Wachowski, starring Keanu Reeves. "Bullet time" was achieved with a ring of 120 still cameras. The concept of a simulated reality — the "red pill / blue pill" — has since migrated into every internet conspiracy subculture.
